issues.legal_issue: A secured creditor may proceed with a subsequent sale notice without providing a fresh full notice period when a properly notified earlier sale was prevented solely by the borrower’s or guarantors’ conduct and the subsequent notice continues the earlier sale process.
material_facts: The initial sale notice provided the prescribed clear notice period and covered four mortgaged properties.
The guarantors obtained an interim stay of the initial sale after representing that they would sell property and pay the bank; they did not pay the full outstanding amount as represented.
After the initial challenge was dismissed, the bank issued a subsequent notice covering the unsold properties, excluding a property already sold by private treaty and revising the outstanding amount.
The guarantors again challenged the subsequent notice and obtained conditional interim protection, but did not make the required deposit.
The bank sold the remaining properties at auction, and the sale was later registered in favour of the successful bidder.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent notice was a continuation of the initial sale process, and a fresh full notice period was not required because the initial sale had been prevented for reasons solely attributable to the guarantors. The challenge to the subsequent notice and sale therefore failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act, read with Rules 8(6) and 9(1) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, requires the prescribed clear notice before a sale. Under Mathew Varghese v. M. Amritha Kumar (2014) 5 SCC 610, if a properly notified sale does not take place for reasons not solely attributable to the borrower, the prescribed sale procedure must be followed afresh. Where the failure is solely attributable to the borrower or guarantors, a subsequent notice continuing the earlier process does not require a fresh full notice period. The Court distinguished Vasu P. Shetty v. Hotel Vandana Palace (2014) 5 SCC 660 and J. Rajiv Subramaniyan v. Pandiyas (2014) 5 SCC 651 on their facts.

predicates.secured_enforcement_sale_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a secured creditor’s enforcement sale of mortgaged property.
predicates.initial_sale_notice_complied_with_notice: The initial sale notice gave the prescribed clear notice period to the borrower or guarantors.
predicates.initial_sale_prevented_solely_by_borrowe: The initial sale did not take place because of conduct or proceedings attributable solely to the borrower or guarantors.
predicates.subsequent_notice_continues_initial_sale: The subsequent notice continues the earlier sale process for property that remains unsold.

issues.definition: When a secured enforcement sale was properly notified but was prevented solely by the borrower’s or guarantors’ conduct, a subsequent notice continuing that sale process may be valid without a fresh full notice period.

issues.legal_issue: The mortgagor’s right to redeem the secured property is extinguished upon registration of the completed sale in favour of the purchaser.
material_facts: The bank was permitted by the tribunal to proceed with the sale after the guarantors failed to satisfy the conditions for interim protection.
The successful bidder paid the sale consideration, and the sale was registered in the purchaser’s favour.
The challenge seeking to set aside the sale was pursued after registration.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagor’s right of redemption had been extinguished upon registration of the sale, and the later challenge could not restore that right or invalidate the sale.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, preserves the right of redemption until it is extinguished by an act of the parties; the right survives a contract for sale until completion of the sale by a registered instrument. Mathew Varghese v. M. Amritha Kumar (2014) 5 SCC 610 applied that principle to secured assets under the SARFAESI Act. Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam (1977) 3 SCC 247 states the underlying rule, and Dwarika Prasad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 5 SCC 491 and Shakeena v. Bank of India (2019) SCC OnLine SC 1059 support extinction of the redemption right upon registration of the sale certificate.

predicates.mortgage_sale_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a sale of mortgaged property conducted by a secured creditor.
predicates.secured_property_sale_registered: The completed sale of the secured property has been registered in favour of the purchaser.

issues.definition: In a proceeding challenging a mortgage sale, registration of the completed sale means that the mortgagor’s right to redeem the property is extinguished.

issues.legal_issue: Surplus proceeds attributable to the sale of a mortgaged property are payable to that property’s owner and mortgagor.
material_facts: The property producing the disputed surplus belonged exclusively to the claimant mortgagor and was sold separately under a later sale notice.
The proceeds from the other mortgaged properties were attributable to separate sales and had been accounted for separately.
The disputed excess amount remained with the bank from the sale of the claimant’s property.
issues.conclusion: The direction requiring the bank to pay the surplus proceeds, with interest, to the owner and mortgagor of the property that generated them was correct.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the sale history and the tracing of the excess proceeds to the particular mortgaged property. It found no basis to treat the surplus as proceeds from all the mortgaged properties and also considered it equitable that the surplus be paid to the owner and mortgagor of the property sold. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this allocation ruling.

predicates.secured_sale_surplus_dispute: The proceeding concerns the allocation of money remaining after a secured creditor’s sale of mortgaged property.
predicates.surplus_traceable_to_specific_mortgaged_: The surplus proceeds are attributable to the sale of a particular mortgaged property rather than to other properties.
predicates.claimant_owns_and_mortgaged_that_propert: The claimant owns the particular property and mortgaged it as security.

issues.definition: When a surplus from a secured sale is traceable to a particular mortgaged property, it is payable to the claimant who owns and mortgaged that property.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may direct delivery of the purchased properties and payment of rent retained by former occupants to give effect to a registered auction sale.
material_facts: The auction purchaser’s sale of the properties had been confirmed and registered.
The former occupants continued to retain possession and receive rent from the properties for years after registration.
The purchaser was consequently unable to enjoy the benefits of the registered sale.
issues.conclusion: The Court invoked Article 142 of the Constitution and directed the appellants to deliver vacant and peaceful possession to the auction purchaser and to pay the rent they had received; it did not award interest on that rent.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice in a cause or matter before it. The Court applied that power to give effect to the registered purchaser’s ownership where the former occupants had retained possession and rent despite the completed sale.

rule.if: supreme_court_sale_enforcement_appeal and purchaser_ownership_registered and former_occupants_retained_possession_or_rent and purchaser_deprived_of_sale_benefits

predicates.supreme_court_sale_enforcement_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal before the Supreme Court concerning enforcement of a secured sale.
predicates.purchaser_ownership_registered: The purchaser’s ownership following the sale has been registered.
predicates.former_occupants_retained_possession_or_: The former occupants continued to possess the property or receive rent after the sale.
predicates.purchaser_deprived_of_sale_benefits: The purchaser was unable to enjoy the benefits of the registered sale.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal concerning an enforcement sale, if registered ownership has not enabled the purchaser to enjoy the property because former occupants retained possession or rent, the Court may order those benefits delivered to the purchaser.
